hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-01.question: Since when have private-sector employers with at least 250 employees (as a rule) been required to have an internal reporting channel under the Hinweisgeberschutzgesetz (HinSchG)?

options.a: Since 1 January 2023
options.b: Since 2 July 2023
options.c: Since 17 December 2023
options.d: Not until 1 January 2025

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-01.explanation: The HinSchG entered into force on 2 July 2023; for employers with at least 250 employees (as a rule) the duty to set up an internal reporting channel applied from that date. 17 December 2023 is the date from which the duty also applied to employers with 50-249 employees, not to the larger companies. 1 January 2023 predates the Act's entry into force.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-02.question: A company regularly employs 80 people. From what date did it have to have an internal reporting channel in place?

options.a: From 2 July 2023, the same as all other companies
options.b: Never - companies with under 250 employees are exempt entirely
options.c: From 17 December 2023, because employers with 50-249 employees had a longer transition period
options.d: Only after a case-by-case review by the Bundesamt für Justiz

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-02.explanation: Employers with 50-249 employees (as a rule) had an extended transition period until 17 December 2023, from which date they too had to have an internal reporting channel in place. There is no blanket exemption for smaller companies, and the Bundesamt für Justiz does not conduct a case-by-case review of whether the duty applies.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-03.question: How do employers with fewer than 50 employees fare regarding the duty to set up an internal reporting channel?

options.a: They are always obliged, as soon as they engage in even one activity subject to reporting duties
options.b: As a rule, they are not obliged to set up an internal reporting channel, apart from a few sector-specific special rules
options.c: They must set up the same reporting channel as companies with 250+ employees, just on a later deadline
options.d: They may permanently opt out of the duty simply by filing a written declaration with the Bundesamt für Justiz

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-03.explanation: The core duty to set up an internal reporting channel under §12 HinSchG is tied to the 250- and 50-employee thresholds; businesses with fewer than 50 employees are, as a rule, not covered, although certain regulated sectors (e.g. financial services) may have separate, independent special duties. There is no opt-out via written declaration to the Bundesamt für Justiz - the external reporting channel remains available regardless of any internal company declaration.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-04.question: How does the internal-reporting-channel duty apply to public-sector employers (e.g. authorities, municipalities)?

options.a: Public-sector employers are entirely exempt, since the HinSchG only applies to the private sector
options.b: Public-sector employers must always set up a reporting channel regardless of size, with no threshold rule at all
options.c: Public bodies are subject to their own rules broadly comparable to the private-sector thresholds, and smaller municipalities may in some cases be grouped together
options.d: Public-sector employers may only have their reporting channel operated directly by the Bundesamt für Justiz

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-04.explanation: The HinSchG does not only cover the private sector - it also obliges public-sector employers to set up internal reporting channels, under their own rules broadly similar to the private-sector thresholds, with special provisions for e.g. smaller municipalities. There is no blanket exemption for the public sector, and no requirement that it be run exclusively by the Bundesamt für Justiz - that body operates the external federal reporting channel, not a given authority's internal channel.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-01.question: What requirement does the HinSchG impose on the person(s) who staff the internal reporting channel?

options.a: They must always be a member of the company's executive management
options.b: They must have the necessary expertise and carry out the role independently and free of conflicts of interest
options.c: They must come exclusively from the company's legal department
options.d: They must first be accredited by the Bundesamt für Justiz before they may act

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-01.explanation: Under §§12-13 HinSchG, the employer must set up a competent, independent internal reporting channel; the people entrusted with it need the expertise the task requires and must be independent and free of conflicts of interest. The law does not require the role to be restricted to executive management or the legal department, and there is no accreditation requirement with the Bundesamt für Justiz for internal reporting channels.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-02.question: May a company outsource the operation of its internal reporting channel to an external ombudsperson or law firm?

options.a: No, the reporting channel must always consist of the company's own employees
options.b: Yes, the task can be assigned to an internal unit or outsourced to an external ombudsperson or law firm, as long as independence and expertise are maintained
options.c: Yes, but only if the company has fewer than 50 employees
options.d: No, outsourcing is only permitted with prior case-by-case approval from the Bundesamt für Justiz

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-02.explanation: The HinSchG expressly allows the internal reporting channel to be operated either by an internal unit or delegated to a third party - such as an external ombudsperson or a law firm - as long as the required independence and expertise are maintained. There is no restriction to the company's own employees, no approval requirement from the Bundesamt für Justiz, and no size limit to small companies for this option.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-03.question: Within what deadline must the reporting channel acknowledge receipt of a report to the whistleblower under §17 HinSchG?

options.a: Within 24 hours
options.b: Within 7 days
options.c: Within 30 days
options.d: Within 3 months

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-03.explanation: §17 HinSchG requires the reporting channel to acknowledge receipt of a report within 7 days. The 3-month period does not apply to this acknowledgement but to the later feedback on planned or taken follow-up measures. 24 hours and 30 days are not the deadlines set by the Act for this step.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-04.question: A manager tells an employee she must report her suspicion internally first - she may only contact the external reporting channel at the Bundesamt für Justiz if the internal channel fails to respond, and disclosing to the press is never protected anyway. What is actually correct?

options.a: Both are correct: internal-before-external is mandatory, and disclosure to the press is never protected
options.b: Whistleblowers can freely choose between the internal and external reporting channel, without first having to try the internal one; disclosure to the public is only protected as a last resort under narrow conditions (e.g. no response from the reporting channels, imminent danger to the public, or risk of retaliation/evidence destruction)
options.c: There is no mandatory order of precedence, but disclosure to the press is always fully protected with no conditions at all
options.d: Internal-before-external is mandatory, whereas disclosure to the press is always protected

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-04.explanation: The HinSchG places the internal and external reporting channel on an equal footing - a person can choose freely, without having to try the internal route first. Disclosure to the public (e.g. the press), by contrast, is protected only as a last resort under narrow, statutorily named conditions, such as no response from the reporting channels, imminent danger to the public interest, or a risk of retaliation or destruction of evidence. Both misconceptions - a forced internal first step and a blanket protected or unprotected view of press disclosure - can in practice deter whistleblowers from choosing the correct channel, which is why this point is considered particularly consequential.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-01.question: Whose identity must the reporting channel treat as confidential, as a rule, under §8 HinSchG?

options.a: Only the whistleblower's identity
options.b: Only the identity of the person the report is directed against
options.c: Both the whistleblower's identity and that of the person implicated or accused in the report
options.d: Nobody's identity - confidentiality is only a non-binding recommendation, not a legal duty

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-01.explanation: §8 HinSchG obliges the reporting channel to keep both the whistleblower's identity and that of the implicated or accused person confidential, subject to narrow, statutorily named exceptions. This is a genuine legal duty, not a mere recommendation, and it is not limited to protecting only one of the two sides.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-02.question: Is the confidentiality duty regarding the whistleblower's identity absolute, with no exceptions at all?

options.a: Yes, the identity may never be disclosed under any circumstances, not even to law enforcement authorities
options.b: No, the Act provides narrowly limited, specifically named exceptions in which disclosure is permitted
options.c: No, any manager may disclose the identity whenever they consider it factually warranted
options.d: Yes, except where the whistleblower has personally requested full anonymity in writing

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-02.explanation: Confidentiality is the rule, but not without exception: the Act names narrowly defined cases in which disclosure is permitted, for example in connection with certain administrative or judicial proceedings. The Act does not grant individual managers a general discretion to disclose - that would undermine the protective purpose of the law.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-03.question: For how long must the reporting channel, as a rule, retain the documentation of a received report before it must be deleted?

options.a: 6 months
options.b: 3 years
options.c: 10 years
options.d: Indefinitely - there is no deletion duty

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-03.explanation: Under §11 HinSchG, documentation of a report must, in essence, be retained for around three years after the procedure concludes and then deleted, unless another legal basis requires or justifies continued storage. Indefinite retention with no deletion duty would run counter to both the data-protection and confidentiality rationale of the Act.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-04.question: An employee working at the reporting channel casually mentions over lunch to a colleague who submitted a particular report, thinking it is harmless office chat. How should this be assessed?

options.a: Not a problem, as long as the information is not shared in writing or by email
options.b: A breach of the confidentiality duty under §8 HinSchG, which can carry a fine and exposes the whistleblower to real risk
options.c: Not a problem, because the confidentiality duty only applies towards external third parties, not within the company
options.d: Only a problem if the colleague in turn passes the information on further

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-04.explanation: The confidentiality duty under §8 HinSchG applies regardless of the communication medium and also applies within the company - a casual verbal disclosure of the identity is just as much a breach as a written one. Such a breach can carry a fine and exposes the whistleblower to exactly the risk (e.g. retaliation from colleagues or superiors) that the Act is meant to protect against - which is why this misunderstanding is particularly dangerous, regardless of whether the information is spread any further.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-01.question: What does §36(1) HinSchG provide regarding retaliation against whistleblowers?

options.a: Retaliation is allowed as long as it does not become publicly known
options.b: Retaliation is only prohibited for reports made to the external reporting channel, not for internal reports
options.c: Retaliation against persons who have made a report or a disclosure is prohibited
options.d: Retaliation is only prohibited if the reported suspicion later turns out to be accurate

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-01.explanation: §36(1) HinSchG prohibits retaliation against persons who have made a report or disclosure within the meaning of the Act, regardless of whether the report was internal or external and regardless of whether the suspicion is ultimately confirmed. What matters is that there were reasonable grounds to believe the report was accurate at the time it was made, not the later outcome of the investigation.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-02.question: An employee reports a violation and shortly afterwards is not promoted as had otherwise been planned. He suspects a connection. Who must prove whether or not there is a connection to the report?

options.a: The whistleblower must fully prove that the missed promotion was retaliation
options.b: The employer must prove that the missed promotion was NOT based on the report - the burden of proof is reversed
options.c: Neither - such cases are decided exclusively by an arbitration body with no burden-of-proof rule at all
options.d: The whistleblower must prove the report was the cause, but only if he reported externally rather than internally

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-02.explanation: Under §36(2) HinSchG, the burden of proof reverses as soon as a whistleblower suffers a detriment after making a report: the employer must then show and prove that the detriment was NOT based on the report. The widespread assumption that the whistleblower must prove the connection himself is exactly backwards and would effectively gut the protection the Act is meant to provide - which is why this is a particularly dangerous misconception, regardless of whether the report was internal or external.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-03.question: What legal consequence attaches to a retaliatory measure taken despite the prohibition in §36 HinSchG - for example, a dismissal issued in reaction to a report?

options.a: It remains fully valid; the whistleblower can only demand an apology
options.b: It is void or has no legal effect, and the whistleblower can additionally claim damages
options.c: It remains valid as long as the employer gives written reasons for it
options.d: It automatically terminates the entire employment relationship in the whistleblower's favour with double salary

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-03.explanation: Under §37 HinSchG, retaliatory measures within the meaning of §36 HinSchG are void or without legal effect; in addition, the whistleblower can claim damages for the harm suffered. The Act does not provide for a mere duty to apologise or an automatic termination of the contract with double salary, and giving written reasons does not cure an unlawful retaliatory measure.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-04.question: Which of the following measures, if taken in reaction to a permissible report, could count as a prohibited retaliatory measure within the meaning of §36 HinSchG? (Select all that apply)

options.a: Transferring the whistleblower to a lower-graded position without objective justification
options.b: A routine, performance-based salary adjustment applied equally to all team members regardless of any report
options.c: Bullying or ostracising the whistleblower by managers after the report becomes known
options.d: A compliance training session offered to all employees in the department

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-04.explanation: Retaliatory measures within the meaning of §36 HinSchG are detriments connected to a report, e.g. an objectively unjustified transfer to a worse position, or bullying/ostracism by managers. A routine salary adjustment applied equally to everyone and a training offer made to the whole department are neutral measures unrelated to the report and do not constitute retaliation.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-01.question: Up to what amount can a fine be imposed if an employer obstructs a report or subjects a whistleblower to a retaliatory measure?

options.a: Up to €5,000
options.d: No fine is provided for this - only civil damages

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-01.explanation: Obstructing a report and taking retaliatory measures against a whistleblower can both be sanctioned with a fine of up to €50,000. This sanction exists alongside the civil-law damages claim under §37 HinSchG, not instead of it.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-02.question: An obligated employer with 300 employees fails to set up any internal reporting channel at all, despite the statutory duty. What is the maximum fine it must expect for this?

options.a: Up to €5,000
options.b: Up to €50,000, the same as for retaliation
options.d: No fine is threatened, only a non-binding administrative warning

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-02.explanation: Completely failing to set up the legally required internal reporting channel can be sanctioned with a fine of up to €20,000 - a lower maximum than for obstructing a report or for retaliation (each up to €50,000), but still a genuine fine, not a mere administrative warning.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-03.question: An employee at the reporting channel breaches the confidentiality of a whistleblower's identity by disclosing it to third parties without legal grounds. What is the maximum fine provided for this?

options.d: Up to €1,000

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-03.explanation: The unauthorised disclosure of a whistleblower's (or an implicated person's) identity can be sanctioned with a fine of up to €50,000 - the same maximum as for obstructing a report and for retaliation, because the Act treats all of these violations as comparably serious.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-04.question: Which of the following statements about the fines under the HinSchG is correct?

options.a: There is a single uniform fine range of €50,000 for all violations named in the Act
options.b: The fine amounts differ depending on the violation - among others, up to €20,000 for entirely failing to set up a reporting channel, and up to €50,000 for obstruction, retaliation, or confidentiality breaches
options.c: Fines under the HinSchG can only be imposed on individual employees, never on the company as a whole
options.d: Fines are only provided for in the HinSchG as a non-binding self-commitment by companies, not as a state-enforceable sanction

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-04.explanation: The HinSchG scales the fine ranges according to the severity and type of violation: up to €20,000 for entirely failing to set up a required internal reporting channel, up to €50,000 for obstructing a report, for retaliation, and for confidentiality breaches. These are genuine, state-enforceable administrative-fine (Ordnungswidrigkeiten) sanctions, not a merely voluntary self-commitment, and they can be directed at the company as a whole, not only at individuals.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-05.question: A credit institution employs only 30 people. Does it still have to set up an internal reporting channel?

options.a: No, because it is below the general 50-employee threshold
options.b: Yes, because certain regulated entities such as credit institutions, securities service providers, and insurance undertakings are obligated regardless of their employee count
options.c: Only if it additionally serves at least 50 customers per year
options.d: No, financial-sector companies are generally exempt from the HinSchG

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-05.explanation: §12(3) HinSchG obliges certain financial-sector entities (e.g. credit institutions, securities service providers, insurance undertakings, capital management companies) to set up an internal reporting channel regardless of their employee count. The general 50-employee threshold in paragraph 2 does not apply to them, and there is no blanket exemption for the financial sector - quite the opposite.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-06.question: Who is protected under the personal scope of the HinSchG?

options.a: Only current employees with a permanent employment contract
options.b: Natural persons who obtained and reported information about violations in connection with their professional activity or in the run-up to one, as well as persons who are the subject of a report or otherwise named in it
options.c: Only persons who have already contacted an external reporting channel
options.d: Only managers who become aware of compliance violations in the course of their duties

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-06.explanation: §1(1) and (2) HinSchG protects natural persons who obtained information about violations in connection with their professional activity - including beforehand, e.g. as job applicants - as well as, in addition, persons who are the subject of a report and other persons named in it. The Act does not limit this to employees on permanent contracts, to managers, or to persons who have already reported externally.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-07.question: Which statement about the material scope of the HinSchG (§2) is most accurate?

options.a: Only criminal offences are covered; mere administrative offences are never included
options.b: Covered are criminal offences as well as certain administrative offences specifically named in the Act (e.g. protecting life, health, or employee rights), plus violations of numerous named EU and national provisions such as data protection, anti-money laundering, or product safety
options.c: Any internal workplace dissatisfaction, e.g. about working hours or team atmosphere, is covered
options.d: Only violations of the GDPR are covered

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-07.explanation: The material scope under §2(1) HinSchG covers criminal offences, certain administrative offences insofar as they serve to protect life, health, or employee rights, and violations of a statutorily enumerated list of EU-law-derived areas such as anti-money-laundering, product safety, environmental protection, or data protection. Purely internal dissatisfaction unrelated to these named areas is not covered, and limiting the scope to the GDPR alone is inaccurate - data protection is just one of many covered areas.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-08.question: A group consists of three legally separate subsidiaries with 80, 90, and 100 employees respectively. How does this affect the HinSchG thresholds?

options.a: The employee numbers of all three companies are added together, automatically triggering the duties for employers with 250+ employees
options.b: Each company is, as a rule, assessed individually for the thresholds; since all three fall in the 50-249 range, they may set up a joint office for receiving reports under §14(2) HinSchG, while remediation measures and feedback remain the responsibility of each individual company
options.c: Only the largest subsidiary must set up a reporting channel, and the others are automatically exempt
options.d: A joint reporting office within a group of companies is generally prohibited by law

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-08.explanation: The thresholds in §12(2) HinSchG attach to the individual employer, not to a group-wide total - there is no aggregation across legally separate companies. Precisely because each company individually falls between 50 and 249 employees, §14(2) HinSchG allows them to operate a joint office for receiving reports; the duty to take remedial measures and give feedback to the whistleblower, however, remains with each individual company. There is no automatic exemption for the smaller companies, nor a general prohibition on joint offices.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-05.question: What requirement does §16(3) HinSchG impose on how reporting channels are designed?

options.a: Reports may only be submitted in writing via a form
options.b: Reporting channels must allow both oral and written reports; on request, an in-person meeting must also be arranged within a reasonable timeframe
options.c: Reports must always be made by video call to verify identity
options.d: Oral reports are legally excluded because they cannot be documented

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-05.explanation: §16(3) HinSchG requires reporting channels to permit both oral (e.g. telephone) and written reports; if the whistleblower requests it, an in-person meeting with a responsible person must also be arranged within a reasonable time. The Act does not require written form only or mandatory video calls, and oral reports are not excluded - they are expressly provided for.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-06.question: Who may access incoming reports under §16(2) HinSchG?

options.a: All employees of the HR department, regardless of their specific role
options.b: Only the persons responsible for receiving and processing reports, and the persons supporting them in that task
options.c: Any manager who asserts a legitimate interest
options.d: The works council automatically and without being asked, for every report

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-06.explanation: §16(2) HinSchG restricts access to incoming reports to the persons responsible for receiving and processing them, plus their support staff. A blanket access right for the whole HR department, for individual managers at their own discretion, or an automatic access right for the works council is incompatible with this.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-07.question: What applies to the reporting channel's feedback on follow-up measures under §17(2) HinSchG?

options.a: It must be given within 24 hours of the report and must fully disclose all internal investigation details
options.b: It must, as a rule, be given no later than three months after the acknowledgement of receipt, though information may be withheld to the extent it would otherwise impair internal investigations or the rights of affected persons
options.c: It is not legally required and is entirely at the discretion of the reporting channel
options.d: It must always be given in writing by registered mail

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-07.explanation: Under §17(2) HinSchG, the reporting channel must, as a rule, provide information within three months of the acknowledgement of receipt (or three months and seven days if no acknowledgement was given) about planned or already-taken follow-up measures and their reasons; information may be withheld, however, to the extent it would otherwise impair internal investigations or the rights of affected persons. A 24-hour deadline with full disclosure of all investigative details, or complete discretion with no deadline at all, does not reflect the Act.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-08.question: A company fully outsources the operation of its internal reporting channel to an external law firm. Who nevertheless remains responsible for taking remedial measures?

options.a: The external law firm alone; the company is fully relieved of responsibility
options.b: The company itself; outsourcing the receipt of reports does not relieve the employer of the duty to take appropriate follow-up measures
options.c: No one - all statutory duties end with the outsourcing
options.d: The Bundesamt für Justiz, which takes over full oversight from that point on

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-08.explanation: §14(1) HinSchG allows delegating the operation of the internal reporting channel to a third party such as an external law firm, but expressly does not relieve the employer of the duty to take appropriate remedial measures itself. The same allocation of responsibility applies correspondingly to the joint office of several employers under §14(2) HinSchG. The idea that outsourcing ends every own duty, or that responsibility fully shifts to the external body or the Bundesamt für Justiz, is incorrect.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-05.question: Who, as a rule, may be told the identity of the whistleblower under §8(1) sentence 2 HinSchG?

options.a: Any member of executive management, upon request
options.b: Only the persons responsible for receiving reports or taking follow-up measures, and the persons supporting them in that task
options.c: The entire workforce, as soon as the report is being processed internally
options.d: Anyone the whistleblower has previously informed orally

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-05.explanation: §8(1) sentence 2 HinSchG expressly limits the circle of persons who may learn the identity to those responsible for receiving reports or taking follow-up measures, and their supporting staff. Automatic knowledge by the whole of executive management or the entire workforce is incompatible with this.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-06.question: A report is received by mistake by an internal reporting channel that is not actually competent for this type of violation. Does the confidentiality duty still apply?

options.a: No, the confidentiality duty automatically lapses once the lack of competence becomes apparent
options.b: Yes, the confidentiality duty applies under §8(2) HinSchG regardless of whether the reporting channel is actually competent for the incoming report
options.c: No, in this case the identity may be passed on informally to any other office
options.d: Yes, but only if the whistleblower has confirmed the lack of competence in writing beforehand

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-06.explanation: §8(2) HinSchG makes clear that the confidentiality duty applies regardless of whether the specific reporting channel approached is actually competent for the incoming report. The common misconception that identity may be passed on informally in case of a lack of competence, or that the duty automatically lapses, is wrong and can directly endanger the whistleblower, e.g. if the identity is informally passed to the affected department - which is why this point is particularly practice-relevant and risk-laden.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-07.question: A whistleblower reports by phone but does not want the call to be recorded. How must the reporting channel proceed under §11(2) HinSchG?

options.a: It may record the call anyway, since the documentation duty takes precedence
options.b: Without consent, it may not create an audio recording or a complete verbatim transcript, and must instead prepare a summary of the content of the call
options.c: It must reject the report, since documentation without a recording is not permitted
options.d: It may secretly record the call, as long as the recording is deleted afterwards

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-07.explanation: §11(2) HinSchG provides that an audio recording or complete verbatim transcript of telephone or other oral reports may only be made with the whistleblower's consent; without consent, a summary of the content must be prepared instead. A recording against the person's will - open or secret - is incompatible with this, and rejecting the report for lack of a recording is likewise not provided for.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-08.question: What right does the whistleblower have regarding the protocol prepared for an in-person meeting under §11(4) HinSchG?

options.a: No right to see the protocol at all
options.b: The right to review the protocol, correct it if needed, and confirm it by signature or other means
options.c: The right to have the protocol fully deleted at any time, even after the procedure has concluded
options.d: The right to demand only a copy in a foreign language

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-08.explanation: Under §11(4) HinSchG, the whistleblower has the opportunity to review the protocol of an in-person meeting, correct it if needed, and confirm it by signature or other means; audio recordings used to prepare it must then be deleted. The Act does not provide a general right for the reporting channel to refuse access, an unrestricted right for the whistleblower to have the protocol itself deleted, or a right to a foreign-language copy.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-05.question: A manager merely threatens an employee with a transfer but ultimately does not carry it out. Is this already a prohibited retaliatory measure within the meaning of §36 HinSchG?

options.a: No, only actually carried-out measures count as retaliation
options.b: Yes, the Act expressly prohibits the mere threat and the attempt of retaliation as well, not only the completed measure
options.c: No, threats fall exclusively under general criminal law, not under the HinSchG
options.d: Yes, but only if the threat was made in writing

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-05.explanation: §36(1) sentence 2 HinSchG makes clear that the prohibition of retaliation also covers threats and mere attempts - actual execution is not required. The assumption that only completed measures are covered misreads the express wording, and the Act does not limit this to written threats.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-06.question: A manager wants to legally safeguard a detriment connected to a report. How can they rebut the statutory presumption of retaliation under §36(2) HinSchG?

options.a: By showing and proving that the detriment was based on sufficiently justified reasons unrelated to the report, or that there was no connection between the report and the detriment
options.b: This is fundamentally impossible - the presumption of retaliation is legally irrebuttable
options.c: By simply denying knowledge of the report, without providing any further evidence
options.d: By requiring the whistleblower to first prove that a connection existed, before the manager has to respond at all

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-06.explanation: Under §36(2) HinSchG, a presumption operates in the whistleblower's favour as soon as they claim a detriment connected to their professional activity and attribute it to the report; the person who caused the detriment must then actively rebut this presumption - either by proving sufficiently justified reasons unrelated to the report, or by proving that there was no connection at all. A mere, unsubstantiated denial is not enough, but the presumption is also not irrebuttable, and the whistleblower must never be required to prove the connection first - that would effectively gut the statutory reversal of the burden of proof, which is why this is a particularly consequential misconception for managers.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-07.question: A rejected job applicant claims that a prior report of a violation at a different employer was the real reason for the rejection, and demands, based on §36 HinSchG, that an employment relationship be established with the employer of his choice. Is this possible?

options.a: Yes, a violation of the retaliation prohibition automatically creates a right to be hired
options.b: No, §37(2) HinSchG makes clear that a violation of the retaliation prohibition does not create a right to establish an employment relationship or to a promotion - a damages claim, however, may come into consideration
options.c: No, because rejected applicants are generally excluded from the scope of the HinSchG
options.d: Yes, but only if the employer has fewer than 250 employees

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-07.explanation: §37(2) HinSchG expressly clarifies that a violation of the retaliation prohibition does not create a right to establish an employment, training, or other contractual relationship, or to a promotion; a damages claim under §37(1) HinSchG may come into consideration instead. Job applicants are generally covered by the personal scope (reports made in the run-up to professional activity), but there is no automatic right to be hired, regardless of company size.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-08.question: A whistleblower intentionally provides false information as an alleged violation in order to harm a colleague. How does the HinSchG classify this case?

options.a: The whistleblower remains fully protected in every case, since the Act generally shields reporting persons from any consequence
options.b: Under §38 HinSchG, the whistleblower is liable to compensate for damage arising from an intentional or grossly negligent report of incorrect information - the Act's special protection does not apply to such false reports
options.c: The Act provides no consequences at all for false reports, neither civil nor otherwise
options.d: The colleague must bear the damage themselves, since the HinSchG does not provide for damages claims between employees

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-08.explanation: §38 HinSchG obliges the whistleblower to compensate for damage arising from an intentional or grossly negligent report or disclosure of incorrect information. The HinSchG's protection is conditional on there having been reasonable grounds to believe the report was accurate at the time it was made; for knowingly false statements made to harm a colleague, that protection does not apply, and the affected colleague's damages claim remains available.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-05.question: One reporting-channel employee carelessly (negligently) discloses a whistleblower's identity, while another does so knowingly (with intent). Do the fine ranges differ?

options.a: No, a uniform maximum of €50,000 applies to both cases
options.b: Yes: intentional or reckless breaches of confidentiality can be sanctioned with up to €50,000, whereas negligent breaches carry only a lower maximum of up to €10,000
options.c: No, negligent breaches carry no fine at all
options.d: Yes, but exactly the other way round - negligence is punished more severely than intent

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-05.explanation: §40(3) HinSchG covers intentional or reckless confidentiality breaches with a fine range of up to €50,000, while §40(4) HinSchG sets a lower range of up to €10,000 for negligent conduct. Negligent breaches are therefore not fine-free, but are sanctioned more leniently than intentional or reckless ones - certainly not the other way round.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-06.question: A person knowingly discloses incorrect information as an alleged violation. Is this fineable under the HinSchG?

options.a: No, the HinSchG provides no sanction for this at all
options.b: Yes, under §40(1) HinSchG this can be sanctioned with a fine of up to €20,000
options.c: Yes, but only with a symbolic fine of at most €500
options.d: Yes, with the same maximum as retaliation (up to €50,000)

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-06.explanation: §40(1) HinSchG declares the knowing disclosure of incorrect information to be fineable, with a maximum of €20,000 under paragraph 6. That is lower than the range for retaliation or obstructing a report (each up to €50,000), but far more than a merely symbolic amount, and there is certainly no complete impunity.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-07.question: An employer attempts to obstruct a report but ultimately fails. Does this attempt remain without consequence under the fine provisions?

options.a: Yes, only completed obstruction is fineable
options.b: No, under §40(5) HinSchG the attempt to obstruct a report (as well as the attempt of retaliation) is also fineable, with the same maximum as the completed act
options.c: No, but the attempt is only sanctioned with a fraction of the maximum amount
options.d: Yes, an attempt can never be sanctioned under administrative-offence law in principle

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-07.explanation: §40(5) HinSchG expressly declares the attempt to obstruct a report, as well as the attempt of retaliation, to be fineable too, at the same maximum of up to €50,000 under paragraph 6 as the completed act. The idea that only completed violations, or that attempts in general, cannot be sanctioned does not hold here.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-08.question: Which of the following statements about the tiered fine ranges under §40(6) HinSchG is correct?

options.a: There are three tiers: up to €50,000 for obstruction, retaliation (including attempt), and intentional or reckless confidentiality breaches; up to €20,000 for entirely failing to set up an internal reporting channel and for knowing false reports; up to €10,000 for the remaining cases, including negligent confidentiality breaches
options.b: There is only a single tier of €50,000 for all violations without exception
options.c: The amount depends exclusively on company size, not on the type of violation
options.d: Attempts are, as a rule, punished more leniently than completed violations, with their own lower range of €5,000

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-08.explanation: §40(6) HinSchG actually tiers the fine ranges into three levels: up to €50,000 for obstructing a report, for retaliation (including attempt), and for intentional or reckless confidentiality breaches; up to €20,000 for entirely failing to set up an internal reporting channel and for knowing false reports; up to €10,000 for the remaining, in particular negligent, cases. A single uniform tier for all violations, a link solely to company size, or a separate, more lenient range specifically for attempts do not exist - attempts are instead sanctioned like completed acts.
